So there are two different things here, there is:

  1. Updating PhysLean to a new version, as described by this issue. This is something only one person has to do.
  2. Once (1) has been done by someone, then everyone has to run 
lake exe cache get; lake build

on merging with master and redownloading PhysLean etc.

I usually end up doing (1) but haven't had chance yet this month as am currently hot-spotting of my phone, and dare not risk downloading Mathlib over 4G. (Recently moved into a new apartment and am not getting internet installed until early September :sad: ). But any help with this is much appreciated

Happy to go over either of these on Wednesday.
(But everyone should only ever have to do (2) at most once a month).

I had been reading this essay from Isaiah Berlin on the concept of Scientific history where he carefully analyzes the distinction between rigor and predictive nature of natural sciences vs the obvious lack of these traits in history as a subject. It's a big essay and I found his framework quite insightful - tendency to generalize vs to particularize, importance of expert judgement, treating falsifications, too-entagled-to-fail, essentially its an essay on what branches of human knowledge can be formalized and which ones cannot be.

I think it is good food-for-thought for physlib to likewise consider what branches or methods of physics can be formalized and which ones cannot, what are the characteristics of a paper or topic that lends it to formalization or does not (I had been grappling with same question in the condensed matter channel - how does an experimental paper get formalized and to what extent??). I hope Berlin's essay gives a good framework on the terms of engangement with this question, it is ofcourse written in an English empiricist tradition to which Berlin belongs

Maybe a suggestion for changing the format of the Physlib Cafe is that we start with somebody presenting for 5 to 10 minutes on something that they've been working on? This might spur conversation in a given direction and might let us all learn something. If anyone thinks this is interesting and wants to take a first turn at this, maybe write a message here. (With the caveat that we can veto anything that might not be interesting e.g. not mainstream physics etc.)

That sounds like a great idea. I can't be ready by this Thursday but could give a contribution on the digitalization of the deep-inelastic scattering literature. Discussion there could be about how I'm building on assumption bundles to handle statements that can't currently be proven in physlib due to missing support but would be able to be proven in the future after adding increased e.g. Feynman diagram support. If managed, this potentially adds a way to engage communities further downstream in the scientific graph.
(these assumptions are mainstream stuff, the assumption bundles are about e.g. standard symmetry properties of hard scattering QCD diagrams and such, not like I'm assuming something exotic)

Discussion there could be about how I'm building on assumption bundles to handle statements that can't currently be proven in physlib due to missing support but would be able to be proven in the future after adding increased e.g. Feynman diagram support.

I'd also be interested in a discussion in the PhysLean cafe about where mathlib ends and where physlib begins... In particular in terms of group theory. Should we stick Pauli matrices, or SU(N) YM generators in mathlib or do they belong in physlib, that kind of thing.
